schools.summary: Henry: the after-improvement of the feast — the comfort of communion kindles a holy zeal against sin, so the people would not go home till the idols were destroyed.

Ellicott glosses the images as maççebôth (pillars) and groves as Ashérîm (sacred fertility-trunks), and reads the enfeebled north as offering no resistance; 'utterly destroyed' = 'so far as to finishing.'

Clarke leaves it uncertain whether zeal or Hoshea's consent carried the reform into Israel; Wesley reads the work in Manasseh as by God's special impulse, Hoshea tolerating the breaking of Baal's images.
Gill fixes the opening 'when all this was finished' — temple cleansed, feast and seven days of rejoicing kept.

outliers.note: Attributes the iconoclasm in Manasseh distinctly to 'the special impulse and direction of God's spirit.'

themes: destroying the idols after the feast
the reform reaching Ephraim and Manasseh

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott trace the courses to the Davidic order (cf. 8:14; Num. 7:5), 'after the mouth of his service' meaning by its prescribed rule, the Levites set for sacrifice and for song in 'the gates of the camps of Jehovah' (1 Chron. 9:18).
Clarke reads 'the tents of the LORD' as the temple itself; Wesley explains the movable name — the priests and Levites 'encamped there,' perhaps hinting the house would shortly be removed.
Gill: the courses as David fixed them and as they stood under Jehoshaphat, since interrupted, now restored to their regular order.
Keil and Ellicott fix the king's portion as the material for the statutory burnt-offerings of Num. 28-29 (morning, evening, sabbath, new moon, set feasts), supplied from the wealth of 32:27-29.
Clarke sees an old royal duty revived (kings from David furnishing the daily sacrifice); Wesley reads it as mercy — the king easing an impoverished people by bearing the cost himself.
Gill: a bounty from Hezekiah's own treasury, over and above the usual, the temple treasury being exhausted and the people brought low.

themes: the king's portion for the offerings

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott ground the portion in the firstfruits and tithes of Exod. 23:19, Lev. 27:30-33, Num. 18; 'encouraged in the law' means 'stick fast unto the law' (châzaq, cf. 2 Sam. 18:9), that ministers might serve undistracted (Neh. 13:10).
Wesley: 'encouraged' = freed from worldly cares, enabled to give up wholly to the study of the law and the teaching of the people.
Gill reads the portion as the tithes and firstfruits appointed by God's law.

Keil notes the odd 'tithe of holy things' finds no exact correspondence in the law (Num. 18:8; Bertheau); Ellicott takes 'children of Israel' here as the Jerusalemites, the firstfruits for priests and tithe for Levites (Num. 18:12, 21).

Clarke keeps 'honey' (offerable to priests though not on the altar, Lev. 2:11); Wesley reads 'dates,' since the law tithes only fruits of tree, earth, and beast, and marks the command widened beyond Jerusalem.
Gill: the command spread from Jerusalem throughout the cities of Judah and was answered on every hand.

debates.question: Is the tithed sweet produce literal 'honey' or 'dates'?

sides.position: honey — offerable to the priests though not burnt on the altar (Lev. 2:11)
dates — as the Hebrew writers understand it, the law tithing only fruit, field, and beast

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes the northern settlers in Judah's cities from the Jerusalemites of v.5, wrestles with 'tithe of holy things' (= heave-offerings, Num. 18:19; the LXX's 'goats' a copyist's slip; a probable lacuna), and renders 'heaps heaps' = many heaps; Keil frames the heaps by Pentecost and Tabernacles.
Wesley: the heaps were the overplus left after the priests and Levites had used what they needed.
Gill drops the supplied 'concerning': when the edict was known in the country towns, they too paid their dues.

outliers.note: Judges 'tithe of holy things' a surprising isolated phrase, suspects a textual lacuna, and traces the LXX's 'tithes of goats' to a slip of aigôn for agiôn.

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes Sivan (May-June, Pentecost/Firstfruits) and Tisri (Sept-Oct, Tabernacles), and notes the curious form lîsôd ('to lay the foundation') met only here (cf. Isa. 51:16).
Clarke (with the Targum) names Sivan and Tisri and the vast grain-collections; Wesley draws the arc from the harvest's beginning to its close at Tabernacles.
Gill names the third month Sivan, the feast of harvest, when barley ended, wheat began, and firstfruits were brought.
Keil reads the blessing as unfeigned thanksgiving over the heaps, the king passing at once to inquire their cause.
Wesley parts the blessing: thanks to God for plenty and for liberal hearts, and praise of the people for their forwardness and faithfulness.
Henry: they thanked God for the providence that gave something to bring and the grace that gave hearts to bring it, and commended the people 'without reproaching them for their former neglects.'
Gill: what they saw were the heaps of tithes and firstfruits.

themes: blessing the LORD and the people
thanks for plenty and for willing hearts

schools.summary: Keil: the king asked not whether the heaps sufficed but how such masses had been piled up; Ellicott fixes the idiom dârash 'al (cf. 2 Sam. 11:3; 1 Sam. 28:7).
Wesley: the king wondered how so little of the provision was spent and such great heaps yet remained.
Gill: he asked how they grew so large, or why the priests let them lie.

themes: a question of cause not sufficiency

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the exclamatory infinitives 'eating and being satisfied and leaving over unto abundance' (cf. Hos. 4:2), reads 'and there is left this great store,' and identifies the cells (léshâkôth, 1 Chron. 9:26); the blessing echoes Mal. 3:10 and Hag. 2:19.
Gill: Azariah the high priest of the line of Zadok, whom Jarchi identifies with the Azariah of Uzziah's day; the heaps kept to show God's plentiful provision, not from covetousness.

debates.question: Is this Azariah the high priest who withstood Uzziah (2 Chron. 26:17)?

sides.position: hardly the same man, who forty years earlier opposed Uzziah

themes: the LORD hath blessed his people

schools.summary: Henry: the holy things laid up carefully, not left in loose heaps — the ant's wisdom of storing in plenty (Prov. 6:8), and good husbandry itself an encouragement to give.
Keil leaves hekîn open (build or make ready), and notes the firstfruits, tithes, and dedicated things brought in 'with fidelity' (19:9) under Cononiah and Shimei.
Clarke: to make granaries for the superabundance.
Gill: to build new chambers or fit up those already standing.

Ellicott parses the deposit (Terûmah/firstfruits, tithe, holy things), 'faithfully' = with honesty (19:9), Shimei 'the next' = second in charge, Cononiah = Kânanyâhû ('Iahu hath established'); Keil sets out the chain of oversight under the king and Azariah.
Gill: the ministers kept nothing back for private use but faithfully laid up the whole.
Clarke: Shimei was 'the next,' assistant to Cononiah.

themes: the heave-offering, tithe, and holy things

schools.summary: Ellicott: the ten are otherwise unknown (though Jehiel and Mahath recur, 29:12), 'under the hand' = under Cononiah's orders, miphqâd unusually of command (usually census, 1 Chron. 21:5), Azariah the nâgîd (1 Chron. 9:11); Keil sets out the ordered descent from king and high priest.
Henry: officers of approved wisdom and faithfulness set over the stores, that moth, rust, and thieves (Matt. 6:20) should not corrupt them.
Gill: the ten were assistants under Cononiah and Shimei, ready to do as ordered.

Ellicott fixes Kore's post (1 Chron. 9:18) and defines the freewill offerings (Deut. 12:17), the Terûmah transferred to the priests (Lev. 7:14), and the most holy things eaten in the sanctuary (Lev. 6:10; 2:3); Keil sets six Levites under him to supply the brethren great and small.
Wesley: the most holy things are the remainders of freewill, sin, and trespass offerings and the shewbread, for the ministers' competent maintenance.
Gill places Kore at the east gate of the temple.

themes: the porter of the east gate
the oblations and most holy things

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'next him' = 'by his hand' (subordinate, 1 Chron. 25:2), the six giving 'honestly' (be'emûnah, in trust) to the brethren in the courses off duty in their towns, great and small = older and younger.

Wesley: the six received and distributed portions to priests resident in their cities while others served at Jerusalem; Clarke notes 'Miniamin' is read 'Benjamin' in several MSS and the ancient versions.
Gill: Kore dealt with the priests at the temple, the six with priests in the country towns.

outliers.note: Flags the textual variant 'Benjamin' for 'Miniamin,' read by several MSS and the Vulgate, Syriac, LXX, and Arabic.

themes: a textual variant in the names

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read the verse as a parenthetic exception: the temple-serving Levites and their registered sons (3+) drew their daily portion in the sanctuary (cf. 8:13; Neh. 11:23), not from Kore's officers, children eating of the sacrifices with their fathers.
Gill (with Kimchi): males from three years, the age a child could be taught to handle the offerings without defiling them; females admitted at no age.

themes: the register of males from three years
the daily portion in the sanctuary

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil read the verse as a parenthesis on the registers — priests by their fathers' houses (clans), Levites serving from twenty years by their courses, citing David's numbering from twenty (1 Chron. 23:24, 27).
Gill: the priests registered by family, the Levites likewise, each given a portion.

themes: the register of priests and Levites

schools.summary: Ellicott resumes the thread from v.15: the Levites kept a register of the ministers' wives and children, and 'sanctified themselves' means they behaved conscientiously (be'emûnah, in trust, 1 Chron. 9:22) toward the hallowed gifts, though the AV may be substantially right.
Henry (with Patrick): 'in faith they sanctified themselves' — the priests served not doubting they should be provided, and so were not made ashamed of their hope.
Wesley: the households were fed from the holy things because the ministers had sequestered themselves from the worldly affairs by which they might have provided for their families.
Gill: all the households genealogized, a portion given to each by number.

debates.question: What is 'in their set office they sanctified themselves in holiness'?

sides.position: they behaved conscientiously / in good faith toward the hallowed gifts
'in faith' they sanctified themselves, serving in confidence of God's provision

themes: sanctified in faith or in fidelity

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott: named officers ('expressed by name,' 28:15) were set in each priestly city to supply the priests and Levites on the pasture-lands outside the towns (Lev. 25:34; Num. 35:5), giving to every male priest and registered Levite.
Henry: the country priests were not overlooked — the preaching priests maintained as well as the sacrificing, those who abode by the stuff as well as those who warred the warfare.
Gill: the priests on their allotted suburb-lands, dwelling there off duty, had their portion like those at Jerusalem.
Keil reads the verse as the conclusion of the whole account; Ellicott glosses ha'emeth ('truth') as faithfulness or sincerity.
Clarke unfolds the three terms as the portrait of a worthy king — Good and doing good, Upright and doing justice, truly Religious and living by revealed truth.
Henry: his zeal reached all Judah, and he aimed sincerely to please God — 'right' agreeable to natural equity, 'truth' to divine revelation and covenant.
Gill: he settled the courses and made provision for the priests and Levites and their families.

themes: a king good, just, and religious

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'commandment' (singular), 'to seek his God' = 'in order to seek,' and sets 'with all his heart' beside 'a perfect heart' (1 Chron. 28:9) and Deut. 6:5; Keil takes the verse as the account's close.
Clarke: 'a thoroughly excellent man,' who saw his duty and did it with zeal — and a prayer that God send such kings.
Henry: what he began he went through with all his heart, and prospered — 'what is undertaken with a sincere regard to the glory of God will succeed at last.'
Gill enumerates the works — cleansing the temple, providing sacrifices, ordering the ministers, caring for their maintenance.
